Problem Statement & Solution Overview Small and medium-sized educational centers (SMEs) face severe intellectual property leakage when lecture videos are downloaded, screen-recorded, and redistributed illegally. Commercial DRM solutions (Widevine, PlayReady) carry prohibitive licensing fees and integration complexity.
SecureLearn solves this using an AWS–Cloudflare Hybrid Serverless architecture:
Media Pipeline: Videos uploaded to Cloudflare R2 trigger Cloudflare Queues and Consumer Workers to coordinate transcoding via AWS Elemental MediaConvert into HLS/DASH formats. Delivery & Access Control: Students authenticate via Amazon Cognito (JWT). AWS Lambda verifies course entitlements in Amazon DynamoDB and issues a short-lived HMAC-SHA256 signed playback token (1-hour TTL), validated at the edge by Cloudflare Workers. Security & Key Management: AWS KMS and AWS Secrets Manager protect API credentials, while AWS CloudTrail logs all audit events. AI & Leak Tracing: AWS EventBridge triggers an Isolation Forest Lambda function every 5 minutes to detect abnormal access patterns and send alerts via Amazon SNS, paired with a JavaScript dynamic watermark displaying the student’s User ID and IP. 2. AMAZON LINUX AMI VS. WINDOWS AMI: WHICH IS THE BETTER CHOICE WHEN CREATING AN EC2 INSTANCE? When creating an EC2 instance on AWS, choosing between Amazon Linux 2023 and Windows Server AMI involves trade-offs regarding usability, system resources, and operating costs.
Key points to know: Windows AMI – Accessible but High Cost: Features a familiar Graphical User Interface (GUI) and management via Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), making it very friendly for beginners. However, it requires substantial hardware resources (at least 2 GB of RAM; t3.micro/nano are discouraged) and includes additional operating system licensing fees. Amazon Linux 2023 – Optimized Performance and Cost: Built specifically for cloud and enterprise applications focusing on security, high stability, and no separate operating system fees. SSH management is lightweight, highly resource-efficient, and does not require desktop interface maintenance. The Linux Learning Curve: Linux requires users to master the command line, file management, and permissions, and may necessitate supplementary tools like MobaXterm, Git, or remote development environments for smooth workflows. Decision Guide: If an application strictly requires Microsoft technologies (such as legacy .NET Framework or IIS), Windows is the definitive choice. Otherwise, for general workloads like web servers, APIs, and Node.js, Amazon Linux 2023 is the preferred choice due to superior cost optimization and long-term automation capabilities. CENTRALIZED MANAGEMENT OF HUNDREDS OF AWS ACCOUNTS SECURELY WITH ORGANIZATIONS & SERVICE CONTROL POLICIES (SCPs) Managing systems under a single AWS Account model poses significant risks of information security breaches and service disruptions as scale grows or when applying automated tools such as AI Agents. To completely resolve this challenge, AWS recommends adopting a Multi-Account strategy combined with AWS Organizations and Service Control Policies (SCPs).
Key points to know: Single-Account Model Risks & Challenges from AI Agents: Consolidating all environments (Dev, Staging, Prod) into a single account easily leads to a complete system crash when an incident occurs. Additionally, operating automated AI Agents without organization-level guardrails can lead to manipulation (Prompt Injection), resulting in wasted costs or accidental deletion of critical resources. AWS Standard Multi-Account Architecture: Clearly separate the Management Account (root account used solely for management/billing), Organizational Units - OUs (such as Security OU, Workload OU), and enforce centralized security boundaries. The Role of Service Control Policies (SCPs): SCPs establish maximum privilege limits applied across individual OUs or member accounts. SCPs help protect audit data (blocking deletion/disabling of CloudTrail), restrict geographic regions (limiting resource provisioning to approved regions only), lock down sensitive resources (S3, RDS), and prevent member accounts from leaving the organization autonomously. Centralized Monitoring: Combine automated log collection via AWS CloudTrail Organizational Trails, configuration management using AWS Config Aggregator, and automated activation of AWS GuardDuty for all newly created accounts. 3-Step Migration Roadmap: (1) Initialize AWS Organizations & centralized SSO login -> (2) Plan OU structures & separate environments -> (3) Tighten SCPs & automate account provisioning using AWS Control Tower. Reference [1] AWS Documentation - Service Control Policies (SCPs) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html) [2] AWS Documentation - Example Service Control Policies (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps_examples.html) [3] AWS Builder Center - Protecting AWS Organization with SCPs (https://builder.aws.com/content/3ItkGyU0Nn5rfYhYQOkbvFiUQ2O/introduction-to-aws-organizations-and-service-control-policies-scps)

content:
AWS Security: Zero Trust & Least Privilege In many traditional network systems, security is often established based on network boundaries. This means that if you are inside the internal network, you are trusted by default. While this approach is quite simple, it is no longer secure enough in a modern cloud environment. If an attacker manages to bypass the outer perimeter, the system can be fully compromised due to the lack of strict protection layers inside. While exploring AWS, I came across some interesting documents regarding the implementation of Zero Trust architecture and the principle of Least Privilege. These articles (including one from AWS Builder Center published in September 2026) dive deep into how to shift from network-based trust to identity-based trust. What I found particularly fascinating is that solving this challenge does not rely on a single service; rather, it combines multiple AWS services into a complete, multi-layered defense system.
THE PROBLEM TO BE SOLVED Imagine a cloud system where services and users constantly interact with one another:
Users accessing internal applications. Microservices connecting to databases. Third-party applications invoking internal APIs. Management devices connecting to servers. If we rely solely on network locations—such as assuming “Any request coming from a Private Subnet is safe by default”—the system could face immense risks. In this scenario, granting permissions based on network location is no longer trustworthy. The solution introduced by AWS is building a Zero Trust security model—never trust anyone or any system by default, regardless of where they are located. AWS ARCHITECTURE AND CORE PRINCIPLES One of the aspects I really like about the Zero Trust model on AWS is how the system divides the defense pipeline into multiple components based on strict principles:
Verify and Authenticate: AWS requires every user and system to continuously prove their identity on a per-request basis rather than logging in just once. The system evaluates context data points such as user identity, location, and device health to grant access. Least Privilege Access: Users or services are granted only the minimum permissions necessary to perform their tasks. AWS IAM Access Analyzer is used to detect over-privileged permissions and refine exact boundaries. Micro-segmentation: Data and systems are divided into small, strictly isolated segments. AWS Transit Gateway and Security Groups are used to isolate sensitive workloads within Amazon VPC. Automation & Monitoring: The system is continuously monitored to detect risks and trigger alerts. AWS GuardDuty and AWS Security Hub continuously analyze events to automatically detect threats or anomalous behaviors. HOW DOES ZERO TRUST WORK? Not all access requests are allowed through easily just because they originate within an internal network. Under this model, the system applies the “Assume Breach” principle—always assuming that the system may already be compromised and restricting all possible attack paths. For example, instead of just checking an IP address like a traditional network:10.0.0.123 The system performs a comprehensive evaluation of the context: Identity: Role App-Backend Action: s3:GetObject Resource: arn:aws:s3:::customer-data Condition: MFA Active = True, Source VPC = vpc-12345 Based on this contextual identity information, the system makes an access decision, even if the IP address belongs to a trusted zone. This is a critical distinction: protection is identity-driven rather than reliant solely on a simple network perimeter. Data encryption and network controls are also strictly enforced to minimize blast radiuses.
KEY TAKEAWAYS The most notable realization after reading these documents is the perspective that Zero Trust is not a off-the-shelf product you can just buy.More importantly, Zero Trust is an architectural mindset that must be deeply engineered into the cloud system. AWS IAM handles core identity management, while other services take responsibility for network segmentation, traffic control, monitoring, and automated incident response.You can visualize a basic workflow as follows:Authentication via IAM → Network Traffic Control via Security Groups/VPC → Event Monitoring via CloudTrail → Threat Analysis & Detection via GuardDuty.Each service addresses a specific problem, but when combined, they form a robust defense in depth mechanism that cannot be easily broken.Through this, I also realized that when building real-world cloud applications, getting code to run successfully is only a small part of the job. The security architecture surrounding those cloud resources plays a vital role in survival.
CONCLUSION The documents on Zero Trust and Least Privilege offered me a very insightful perspective on re-architecting security on AWS. Instead of building a large external firewall and letting everything inside communicate freely, AWS guides us on how to continuously verify and minimize access privileges for every single service. In particular, combining Identity Management and Networking completely eliminates the biggest weaknesses of traditional security models. In my opinion, this is a essential mindset to explore for anyone learning AWS or DevOps who wants to apply security principles directly into real-world enterprise scenarios.

title: Proposal
content:
SecureLearn: Digital Content Protection System for Educational Platforms — AWS Well-Architected Standards Digital Content Protection System for Educational Platforms — AWS Well-Architected Standards 1. Executive Summary Project Name: SecureLearn (First Cloud Journey - FCAJ Internship Program)
Architecture Standards: AWS Well-Architected Framework (6 Pillars) & AWS-Native Serverless
SecureLearn is a low-cost video content protection solution designed for small and medium-sized educational centers (SMEs). The platform combines AWS for authentication, authorization, video processing, AI, and business logic with Cloudflare for frontend hosting, storage, and content distribution. It converts lecture videos into HLS, controls access using JWT and short-lived playback tokens, and integrates behavioral AI analysis with dynamic watermarking to protect and trace educational intellectual property.
2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? In the era of digital education, small and medium-sized educational centers (SMEs) and online learning platforms face severe intellectual property leakage risks as lecture videos are downloaded, screen-recorded, and redistributed illegally on social media. Large-scale commercial DRM solutions (such as Google Widevine and Microsoft PlayReady) involve high licensing costs and integration complexity, making them financially unfeasible for most SMEs.
The Solution SecureLearn utilizes an AWS-Cloudflare Hybrid Serverless Architecture. It automates video processing via AWS Elemental MediaConvert, manages access control using API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB, and leverages Cloudflare R2, Workers, and CDN for secure distribution. Key features include JWT authentication, short-lived playback tokens, Isolation Forest AI anomaly detection via Lambda and EventBridge, dynamic watermarking, and automated alerts via Amazon SNS.
Comparative Table of Current Issues, Business Impacts, and AWS Solutions:
Current Issue Business Impact SecureLearn Solution (AWS / Cloudflare) Videos downloaded & illegally shared Revenue loss, leakage of exclusive lecture IP HLS/DASH encryption via AWS Elemental MediaConvert combined with JWT authentication Lack of proactive monitoring Failure to detect account sharing or video crawling in real-time Automated Lambda Isolation Forest AI model scanning logs with SNS alerts Inability to trace leaks Unable to identify culprits when videos are screen-recorded Dynamic Watermark displaying User ID & IP directly on the video player High commercial DRM costs SMEs cannot afford infrastructure upkeep Hybrid Serverless architecture using AWS for control plane and Cloudflare for media plane, reducing operational costs and avoiding traditional servers Benefits and Return on Investment The solution eliminates traditional server maintenance, drastically reducing operational expenses compared to commercial DRM platforms. It protects exclusive educational assets, prevents unauthorized sharing, provides active anomaly monitoring, and traces content leaks via dynamic watermarking, all while keeping estimated monthly infrastructure costs around $46 USD.
3. Solution Architecture The system is built on an AWS-Cloudflare Hybrid Serverless Architecture, completely eliminating traditional servers and divided into 4 main functional layers:
Media Pipeline (Upload & Processing): Cloudflare R2 (Source Bucket) stores raw videos with AES-256 at-rest encryption; R2 Event Notifications trigger Cloudflare Queues; Consumer Workers coordinate video transfer to AWS Elemental MediaConvert; MediaConvert outputs HLS/DASH manifests (.m3u8 / .mpd). Delivery & Access Control: Students log in via Cognito and receive JWTs; Lambda License Service verifies entitlements in DynamoDB and requests short-lived signed tokens from Cloudflare; Cloudflare Workers validate tokens before serving private HLS/DASH segments from R2 via CDN. Security & Key Management: AWS KMS protects credentials and secrets used by Lambda; MediaConvert requires signed URLs (requireSignedURLs); AWS CloudTrail records audit logs. AI & Tracing: Offline training using Isolation Forest in Jupyter Notebooks (.pkl model stored in R2); AWS Lambda (triggered by EventBridge every 5 mins) reads access logs from DynamoDB/CloudWatch, runs anomaly inference, and publishes alerts via Amazon SNS; JavaScript-based dynamic watermarks display moving user IDs. Data Flow Diagrams:
Upload Flow: User → API Gateway → Upload Lambda → R2 (Private Source) → R2 Event Notification → Cloudflare Queue → Consumer Worker → AWS MediaConvert → HLS/DASH → Cloudflare CDN → Student. Playback Flow: User → JWT → API Gateway → Authorization Lambda → DynamoDB check → AWS Elemental MediaConvert + Cloudflare R2/Workers Signed Token → HLS/DASH Player → Dynamic Watermark. AI Branch Flow: Authorization/Application Logs → CloudWatch/DynamoDB → EventBridge (every 5 min) → Lambda Anomaly Detection → Isolation Forest → Anomaly detected → SNS → Admin Email. General diagram architecture: AWS Services Used AWS Elemental MediaConvert: Transcodes raw videos into HLS/DASH streaming formats. AWS Lambda & Amazon API Gateway: Handle upload handling, license verification, JWT authorization, and AI anomaly detection logic. Amazon DynamoDB: On-demand NoSQL storage for sessions, DRM logs, and metadata. Amazon CloudWatch & AWS CloudTrail: Centralize audit trails and application logs. AWS KMS & AWS Secrets Manager: Secure cryptographic keys and API tokens. Amazon SNS: Broadcasts automated email alerts to administrators upon detecting anomalies. AWS EventBridge: Triggers the AI anomaly detection Lambda function every 5 minutes. Cloudflare R2, Workers, Queues, & CDN: Provide object storage, event routing, queue decoupling, edge security, and fast content delivery. Evaluation Against 6 AWS Well-Architected Pillars Pillar Implementation Design AWS / Cloudflare Services Used Security Least privilege IAM roles; at-rest (AES-256) and in-transit (TLS 1.3) encryption; secrets managed via AWS Secrets Manager; perimeter defense via Cloudflare WAF and Zero Trust Access. AWS IAM, KMS, Secrets Manager; Cloudflare WAF, Access Reliability Cloudflare Queues decouple upload events from processing; Lambda retry mechanisms; R2 data durability of 11 nines (99.999999999%); industrial-grade transcoding via MediaConvert. Cloudflare R2, Queues, AWS Lambda, EventBridge Operational Excellence Centralized logging via CloudWatch Logs and CloudTrail; automated anomaly alerting via CloudWatch Alarms and Amazon SNS. Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail, SNS, Cloudflare Logpush Performance Efficiency Auto-scaling with Serverless Lambda & API Gateway; optimized video delivery via global Cloudflare CDN and Edge Caching; high-speed parallel MediaConvert transcode. AWS Lambda, MediaConvert, API Gateway, Cloudflare CDN Cost Optimization Pay-as-you-go serverless model; leverage AWS Free Tier and Cloudflare Free Plan; R2 Zero Egress Fee to minimize data transfer costs. AWS Free Tier, Cloudflare R2 (Zero Egress), Free Plan Sustainability Optimized energy consumption using shared AWS serverless infrastructure and Cloudflare edge networks, avoiding idle server waste. AWS Serverless Stack, Cloudflare Edge Network 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Scope:
In-Scope: HLS video protection, JWT user authentication, short-lived playback tokens validated by Cloudflare Workers, HLS/DASH distribution from private R2 buckets, automated DynamoDB/CloudWatch log analysis, and SNS alerts. Out-of-Scope: PDF/Word document protection, hardware DRM integration (HDCP), and real-time livestream video processing. Implementation Phases:
Week 1: Research MediaConvert, R2, KMS, Lambda; design AWS + Cloudflare hybrid architecture; setup AWS and Cloudflare accounts, and dev environments. Week 2: Setup Cloudflare R2 bucket and Workers; write upload Lambda triggers; configure MediaConvert HLS/DASH job templates; build basic React + HLS.js video player. Week 3: Implement Lambda License Service for JWT/entitlement verification and token issuance; integrate Cloudflare Signed URLs & Zero Trust Access; build Admin Portal and DynamoDB metadata APIs. Week 4: Test token lifecycles and expiration; train Isolation Forest model locally, serialize to .pkl, and upload to Cloudflare R2 (models/ prefix); write anomaly detection Lambda; create 5-minute EventBridge rule; integrate CloudWatch + SNS; develop dynamic watermarking. Week 5: Integrate dynamic watermarking into video player; build watermark leakage tracing tools; perform internal security pen-testing (video downloading, account sharing tests); optimize costs and check AWS Budgets. Week 6: Fix bugs, refine UI/UX, record demo video (5-7 mins), write technical blog, finalize workshop lab guide, and prepare presentation slides. 5. Timeline & Milestones Week 1: Architecture design, account setup, and theoretical research. Week 2: Media pipeline setup and automated video transcoding. Week 3: Access control, JWT authentication, and secure playback integration. Week 4: AI anomaly detection integration and token lifecycle testing. Week 5: Dynamic watermarking integration and security penetration testing. Week 6: Bug fixing, demo recording, documentation, and final presentation. 6. Budget Estimation Total estimated monthly infrastructure cost is ~$46 USD/month (simulated with 100 storage hours + 100 viewed hours/month).
Note: Actual costs vary based on usage, region, pricing plans, and AWS Free Tier eligibility.
Infrastructure Cost Breakdown:
Cloudflare R2: ~$1.20 (100 GB storage, 50k requests, Zero Egress) Cloudflare Pages: $0.00 (React frontend hosting) Cloudflare Workers & Queues: $0.00 (Free Plan) Amazon Cognito: $0.00 (User Pool authentication) Cloudflare Zero Trust (Access): $0.00 (Admin portal protection, up to 50 users) AWS MediaConvert: ~$45+ (100 input hours / 6,000 transcode minutes at ~$0.0075/min Basic AVC tier) AWS Secrets Manager: ~$0.40 (API tokens and credentials) AWS KMS: ~$1.15 (Customer Managed Key for secrets encryption) AWS Lambda: $0.00 (Covered by Free Tier for 50k invocations) Amazon API Gateway: ~$0.10 (20k REST API calls) Amazon DynamoDB: $0.00 (On-Demand Free Tier) Amazon CloudWatch: ~$0.75 (Audit logs and alarms) AWS EventBridge: $0.00 (Triggering anomaly detection every 5 mins) Resource Clean-up Plan:
AWS: Delete Lambda functions, API Gateways, DynamoDB tables, SNS topics, EventBridge rules, KMS keys, Secrets Manager secrets, and CloudWatch Log Groups. Cloudflare: Manually delete all videos, R2 bucket objects, Workers, Queues, and Zero Trust configurations after recording the demo. 7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix & Mitigation Strategies:
R2 and AWS Lambda integration complexity (Medium impact, medium probability): R2 is S3-API compatible, enabling AWS SDK usage. Use Cloudflare Workers or polling for triggers. AWS MediaConvert lacks full native DRM (High impact, low probability): Clearly define scope around secure video access, anti-sharing, and traceability. Enable requireSignedURLs, short-lived tokens, and watermarks. MVP does not equal Widevine/PlayReady/FairPlay. Signed Token leakage or incorrect expiration (Medium impact, medium probability): Set short TTLs (1 hour), limit concurrent device sessions, and combine with AI anomaly detection. AI model false-positive predictions (Medium impact, medium probability): Start with Isolation Forest, tune contamination thresholds properly, and log false-positives for periodic retraining. Short internship duration (6 weeks) (High impact, low probability): Prioritize MVP first: Upload → Process → Authorization → Secure Playback, then integrate AI and watermarks. Cost overruns (Medium impact, low probability): Setup strict budget alerts on both AWS and Cloudflare. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements: Automated secure media processing pipeline, hybrid serverless architecture implementation, and automated AI anomaly detection.
Long-Term Value: Provides a cost-effective, scalable digital content protection framework that empowers small and medium educational platforms to safeguard intellectual property without excessive commercial expenses.

title: Edge Playback Authorization Worker
content: Step 1: Create Edge Authorization Worker Go to Cloudflare Dashboard > Workers & Pages > Create application > Create Worker. Name: SecureLearn-EdgeAuth. Bind your private HLS/DASH R2 bucket to the Worker (e.g., variable name VIDEO_BUCKET) and add PLAYBACK_SIGNING_SECRET as an encrypted Worker secret. Step 2: Implement Token Verification Logic Intercept incoming HTTP requests for .m3u8 manifests and .ts / .m4s video segments. Extract the short-lived token and expiration timestamp from query parameters or custom headers. Recompute the HMAC-SHA256 signature and verify: Signature matches PLAYBACK_SIGNING_SECRET. Current timestamp is strictly less than the token’s expiration (exp). Requested video path matches the authorized video ID in the token payload. If valid, fetch the object directly from env.VIDEO_BUCKET and stream it with zero egress fees; otherwise, return HTTP 403 Forbidden. Step 3: Configure Custom Route Open the Worker’s Triggers tab > Add route. Map the route video.yourdomain.com/* to SecureLearn-EdgeAuth.

title: AI Anomaly Detection & Alerting
content: Step 1: Package Lambda Layer for Isolation Forest Dependencies Train the Isolation Forest anomaly detection model offline on simulated access logs and serialize it to model.pkl. Step 2: Create AI Anomaly Detection Lambda Create a new Lambda function named SecureLearn-AnomalyDetection using Python 3.12 runtime and attach the Lambda Layer from Step 1. Implement inference logic: Download model.pkl from Cloudflare R2 via the S3-compatible SDK. Query recent playback/token logs from Amazon DynamoDB or CloudWatch Logs (checking IP diversity, request frequency, and concurrent sessions). Run model.predict() to flag anomalous accounts. If anomalies are detected, publish an alert payload to Amazon SNS. Step 3: Create Amazon SNS Alert Topic Open Amazon SNS > Topics > Create topic > Standard. Name: SecureLearn-AnomalyAlerts. Create an Email subscription with the administrator’s email address and confirm the subscription link sent to the inbox. Step 4: Schedule Periodic Scans via EventBridge Go to Amazon EventBridge > Schedules > Create schedule. Schedule name: SecureLearn-AI-Scan-Schedule. Schedule pattern: Regular rate of rate(5 minutes). Target: Select Lambda function SecureLearn-AnomalyDetection and click Create schedule.

title: Workshop
content:
SecureLearn: A Digital Content Protection System for Educational Platforms In this workshop, you will build SecureLearn, a cost-effective video content protection solution designed for small and medium-sized educational centers (SMEs). The architecture utilizes a Hybrid Serverless model, combining AWS—which handles authentication, authorization, video transcoding, AI-based anomaly detection, and business logic—with Cloudflare, which manages interface hosting, object storage, edge-based token authentication, and CDN distribution (with no egress bandwidth costs).
